0:
When Numbers opens, Israel has been camped at the foot of Mount ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧ for almost a year. They arrived there in the third month after leaving ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, a crowd of freed slaves still astonished by the plagues and the crossing of the sea. At the mountain God gave them his covenant and his law. They built the tabernacle, the portable tent where his presence would dwell among them, and the book of Leviticus recorded the sacrifices, the priesthood and the laws of holiness that would govern life around it. Now, one month after the tabernacle was raised, the time has come to leave the mountain and march toward the land God promised to ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧, ⟦p:isaac_616|Isaac⟧ and ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧.

The English title comes from the old Greek translation of the Bible, which named the book after the two great counts of Israel's fighting men that stand near its beginning and its end. The Hebrew title is more evocative. It is taken from the book's opening line and means in the wilderness, and that is where almost the whole book takes place. It covers close to forty years, from the second year after the exodus to the fortieth, and it carries Israel from ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧ to the very edge of ⟦l:canaan_272|Canaan⟧.

Like the books before it, Numbers does not name its author. Jewish and Christian tradition has linked it with ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, and the book itself says that Moses recorded the stages of Israel's march. It belongs to the Torah, the five books that form the foundation of the Old Testament, and it reads as a continuation of Exodus and Leviticus, with the same leaders: Moses, the reluctant prophet who speaks with God face to face; his brother ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧, the high priest; and their sister ⟦p:miriam_2087|Miriam⟧. Alongside them stand younger men who will matter later, especially ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ son of ⟦p:nun_2214|Nun⟧, Moses' assistant, and ⟦p:caleb_537|Caleb⟧ of the tribe of Judah.

The book moves through three settings. The first ten chapters take place at ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧. The tribes are counted and arranged around the tabernacle, the Levites are given their duties, and the camp is prepared like an army about to march. Then the cloud lifts from the tabernacle and Israel sets out.

The middle of the book follows them through the wilderness, the dry, rugged country of the ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧ peninsula and the ⟦l:negeb_885|Negev⟧, the arid south of ⟦l:canaan_272|Canaan⟧. Almost at once the complaints begin: about the hardship, about the food, about ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ himself. They reach the oasis of ⟦l:kadesh_661|Kadesh⟧, on the southern edge of the promised land, and twelve men are sent to explore it. Ten return frightened, and the people refuse to go in. It is the great turning point of the book. God declares that the generation who came out of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ will die in the wilderness, and that only their children, with ⟦p:caleb_537|Caleb⟧ and ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧, will enter the land. The years that follow are passed over almost in silence, broken only by rebellion, plague and the deaths of ⟦p:miriam_2087|Miriam⟧ and ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧.

The final section is set on the plains of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ River, opposite ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧. A new generation has grown up. Israel defeats the kings who stand in its way, and the king of Moab hires a famous seer named ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ to curse them, with results he did not expect. A second census counts the people who will actually enter ⟦l:canaan_272|Canaan⟧, and ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ is appointed to succeed ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧. The book closes with arrangements for the land itself: how it will be divided, where its borders will run, and how its towns will be shared.

Numbers mixes story and law more freely than any book of the Torah. A narrative of rebellion is followed by instructions about offerings, as if to say that the promise still stands and the life of worship will go on. Its people are painfully recognisable: tired, frightened, nostalgic for ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, quick to blame their leaders. Even ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ fails at a critical moment. Yet through it all the cloud of God's presence goes before them, the manna falls each morning, and the God who brought them out of Egypt keeps leading them on.

Later Scripture returned to these chapters often. The psalms remember the wilderness years, and in the New Testament ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ and the letter to the Hebrews all draw on events in this book. When Numbers ends, Israel is waiting on the plains of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, and the book of Deuteronomy records the words ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ speaks to them there, before they cross the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ without him.
1:
The book begins with a date and a place. It is the first day of the second month of the second year after the exodus, and the Lord speaks to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ in the Tent of Meeting, in the Wilderness of ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧. The tabernacle has stood in the middle of the camp for one month.

⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ receives an order that sounds military, because it is. He and ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ are to count every man twenty years old or more who is able to serve in Israel's army, tribe by tribe. A leader from each tribe is named to help them, and these names will return in the chapters ahead.

The census itself is set out in a steady, formal pattern, the same words repeated for each of the twelve tribes, with ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧'s line counted as two, ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧ and ⟦p:manasseh_1928|Manasseh⟧. The total is large, and its meaning is plain: the family of seventy who went down into ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ has become a nation. One tribe is deliberately left out. The Levites are not to be counted for war. Their task is to carry the tabernacle, set it up, take it down and camp around it as its guardians.
2:
The fighting men have been counted, and now they are arranged. This chapter gives the plan of the camp, and it is drawn with the precision of a military diagram.

At the centre stands the Tent of Meeting. Around it, at a distance, the twelve tribes camp in four groups of three, each under its own standard and family banners. Judah takes the place of honour on the east, toward the sunrise, where the entrance of the tabernacle faces, with ⟦p:issachar_645|Issachar⟧ and ⟦p:zebulun_3002|Zebulun⟧ beside it. ⟦p:reuben_2429|Reuben⟧, ⟦p:simeon_2741|Simeon⟧ and ⟦p:gad_1262|Gad⟧ camp on the south, ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, ⟦p:manasseh_1928|Manasseh⟧ and ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧ on the west, and ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧, ⟦p:asher_337|Asher⟧ and ⟦p:naphtali_2149|Naphtali⟧ on the north. The Levites travel in the middle, with the tabernacle.

The same order governs the march. Judah's camp sets out first and ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧'s camp last. The tribal leaders and numbers from the census are repeated, group by group. The picture is of a people organised around the presence of God, with the Lord's dwelling quite literally at the heart of their life.
3:
With the twelve tribes in their places, attention turns to the tribe that was set apart: ⟦p:levi_1820|Levi⟧. The chapter opens by recalling ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s four sons. ⟦p:nadab_2128|Nadab⟧ and ⟦p:abihu_33|Abihu⟧ died in the ⟦l:sinai_1098|wilderness of Sinai⟧ when they offered unauthorised fire before the Lord, an event told in Leviticus, and so only ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧ and ⟦p:ithamar_649|Ithamar⟧ now serve as priests beside their father.

The Levites are given to ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ as assistants. They do not serve as priests themselves, but they guard and care for the tabernacle on behalf of the whole people. The reason given reaches back to the night of the exodus. When God struck down the firstborn of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, he claimed every firstborn of Israel as his own. Now he takes the Levites in their place.

The Levites are counted, every male a month old or more, by their three clans, descended from ⟦p:levi_1820|Levi⟧'s sons ⟦p:gershon_1305|Gershon⟧, ⟦p:kohath_1790|Kohath⟧ and ⟦p:merari_2004|Merari⟧. Each clan is given a side of the tabernacle to camp on and a share of its care. Then the firstborn of Israel are counted too, and the two totals are compared. The few firstborn left over are redeemed with a payment of silver, given to ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and his sons.
4:
The Levite clans now receive their working orders. A second count is made, this time only of men between thirty and fifty years old, the age of those who will actually do the heavy work of moving the tabernacle.

The Kohathites come first, and their duty is the most sacred and the most dangerous. They carry the holiest objects: the ark of the Testimony, the table of the Presence, the lampstand and the altars. Before they may approach, ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and his sons must go in, take down the veil, and wrap each object in its coverings of blue, scarlet and purple cloth and fine leather. The Kohathites must not touch the holy things or even look at them, or they will die. ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧, Aaron's son, oversees the oil, the incense and the whole tabernacle.

The Gershonites carry the curtains, coverings and screens, and the Merarites the frames, posts, bases, pegs and ropes, both under the direction of ⟦p:ithamar_649|Ithamar⟧, ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s younger son. By the end of the chapter every part of the tabernacle has someone appointed to carry it.
5:
The camp has been ordered around the tabernacle. Now the Lord speaks about keeping that camp fit for his presence, because, as he says, he dwells among them.

Anyone made unclean by a skin disease, a bodily discharge or contact with a dead body, man or woman alike, is to live outside the camp for a time, so that the place where God dwells is not defiled. Anyone who wrongs another person is to confess, repay in full and add a fifth, because a wrong against a neighbour is also unfaithfulness toward the Lord.

The longest section turns to a husband seized by jealousy, who suspects his wife of adultery when there is no witness and no proof. The matter is not left to rumour or to his anger. He brings her to the priest at the sanctuary, and there, before the Lord, she holds an offering in her hands, takes a solemn oath, and drinks holy water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor. The suspicion is settled before God, not by the husband alone.
6:
From the purity of the whole camp, the instructions turn to individuals who choose to give themselves to the Lord in a special way. This is the vow of the Nazirite, from a Hebrew word meaning separated or consecrated, and it is open to men and women alike.

For the length of the vow, a Nazirite avoids wine and anything from the grapevine, lets the hair grow uncut, and stays away from dead bodies, even those of close family. The chapter explains what happens if the vow is broken by accident, when someone dies suddenly nearby, and how it is brought to a close with offerings at the Tent of Meeting, when the consecrated hair is shaved and burned. Later in Israel's history, ⟦p:samson_2468|Samson⟧ and ⟦p:samuel_2469|Samuel⟧ will be dedicated in a similar way from birth.

The chapter ends with some of the best-known words in the Bible. The Lord gives ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and his sons the words with which they are to bless the people of Israel, three short lines that ask the Lord to bless and keep them, to make his face shine on them, and to give them peace. Through this blessing, the Lord says, they will put his name on the Israelites.
7:
This chapter steps back in time. It returns to the day, a month before the census, when ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ finished setting up the tabernacle and anointed it and all its furnishings. On that occasion the twelve tribal leaders, the same men who helped with the count, came forward with gifts.

Their first gift is practical: six covered carts and twelve oxen, given to the Levites for moving the tabernacle. The Gershonites and Merarites, who carry the heavy curtains and frames, receive them. The Kohathites receive none, because the holiest objects are to be carried on their shoulders.

Then, for the dedication of the altar, the leaders bring their offerings one at a time, a tribe a day for twelve days, beginning with ⟦p:nahshon_2144|Nahshon⟧ of Judah. It is the longest chapter in the Torah, and the reason is that each leader's gift is identical and each is recorded in full: silver platter, silver bowl, gold dish of incense, and animals for sacrifice. Each tribe is given its own day and its own full record, and none is reduced to a footnote. The chapter ends quietly, with ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ entering the Tent of Meeting and hearing the voice of the Lord speaking to him from above the ark.
8:
The dedication of the altar is complete, and the narrative turns first to the light inside the sanctuary. ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ is instructed to set up the seven lamps of the golden lampstand so that they shine forward, and the chapter recalls that the lampstand was hammered from gold to the pattern God showed ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ on the mountain.

Then the Levites, who have been counted and given their duties, are formally set apart for service. They are sprinkled with the water of purification, shave their bodies and wash their clothes. The whole congregation gathers, and the Israelites lay their hands on the Levites, a sign that this tribe now stands before the Lord on behalf of all the others. ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ presents them as a wave offering, a gesture usually performed with a sacrifice held up before the altar, here applied to a whole tribe of living people.

The reason is repeated from earlier: the Levites are taken in place of Israel's firstborn, whom God claimed on the night of the exodus. The chapter closes with the ages of service. The Levites begin work at twenty-five, retire from heavy duties at fifty, and afterwards may still assist their younger brothers.
9:
Like the dedication of the altar, the opening of this chapter looks back a little. It is the first month of the second year, a full year since the night Israel left ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, and the Lord tells ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ that the people are to keep the Passover at its appointed time, on the fourteenth day of the month. It is the first anniversary of their deliverance.

A practical problem arises. Some men have become unclean through contact with a dead body, and so they cannot take part. They come to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and ask why they should be shut out. Moses does not answer on his own authority. He waits to hear from the Lord, and the answer establishes a second Passover, a month later, for anyone who is unclean or away on a journey. Foreigners living among Israel may also keep it on the same terms.

The second half of the chapter describes the cloud over the tabernacle, which looks like fire by night. When it lifts, Israel sets out. When it settles, they camp, whether for a night, a few days, a month or longer. Israel is about to leave ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧, and there is no doubt who will be leading.
10:
Israel's long stay at ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧ is about to end. First ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ is told to make two silver trumpets. Their blasts will summon the congregation or its leaders, signal each camp to set out, sound the alarm in battle, and mark the feasts and the new moons.

Then, on the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, the cloud lifts from the tabernacle. Israel has been at the mountain for nearly eleven months. For the first time the camp marches in the order laid out in the opening chapters: Judah first, with ⟦p:nahshon_2144|Nahshon⟧ in command, the tabernacle and its carriers in the middle, ⟦p:dan_973|Dan⟧ bringing up the rear. Their direction is the ⟦l:paran_921|Wilderness of Paran⟧, the vast, dry region to the north, toward ⟦p:canaan_914|Canaan⟧.

Before they go, ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ appeals to ⟦p:hobab_1537|Hobab⟧, the son of his Midianite father-in-law, here called ⟦p:jethro_2431|Reuel⟧, to come with them as a guide who knows where to camp in the desert. The chapter does not record his final answer. It ends with the ark going ahead of the people, and with the words Moses spoke each time it set out and each time it came to rest.
11:
The march has begun, and the chapters of careful order give way to something else. Soon after leaving ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧, the people start to complain. From here on, much of the story of Israel in the wilderness will be a story of complaint, rebellion and God's patience under strain.

The first outbreak is brief. Fire from the Lord burns the edge of the camp until ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ prays, and the place is named ⟦l:taberah_1127|Taberah⟧, burning. Then a larger crisis begins among the rabble, the mixed crowd that came out of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ with Israel. They crave meat, and soon the whole people are weeping in their tents, remembering the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic of Egypt, and despising the manna God sends each morning.

What follows shows ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ at breaking point. He tells the Lord the burden of this people is too heavy for him and asks to die. God answers in two ways. He shares the weight of leadership by placing his Spirit on seventy elders, and he promises the people meat until they are sick of it. ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ son of ⟦p:nun_2214|Nun⟧, Moses' assistant since his youth, steps briefly into view, protective of his master's authority. And it ends with a name that will be remembered: ⟦l:kibroth-hattaavah_685|Kibroth-hattaavah⟧, the graves of craving.
12:
The people have moved on to ⟦l:hazeroth_544|Hazeroth⟧, and now the challenge to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ comes from inside his own family. His sister ⟦p:miriam_2087|Miriam⟧, the prophetess who led the women in song after the crossing of the sea, and his brother ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧, the high priest, begin to criticise him. The spark is Moses' marriage to a Cushite woman. Cush is the land that lies to the south of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧.

The marriage, though, is only the occasion. The real complaint comes out at once: has the Lord spoken only through ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧? Has he not spoken through us too? Scripture pauses here to say of Moses himself that he was very humble, more than anyone on the face of the earth, as if to explain why he says nothing in his own defence.

Instead the Lord intervenes. He summons all three to the Tent of Meeting and speaks of what sets ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ apart from every other prophet. The consequences fall on ⟦p:miriam_2087|Miriam⟧, and the chapter ends with the whole camp waiting for her before they move on into the ⟦l:paran_921|Wilderness of Paran⟧.
13:
Israel is now camped in the ⟦l:paran_921|Wilderness of Paran⟧, at the southern edge of the land God promised, and the oasis of ⟦l:kadesh_661|Kadesh⟧ will be their base.

At the Lord's command, ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ sends twelve men to explore ⟦l:canaan_272|Canaan⟧, one leader from each tribe. Two names stand out from the list. ⟦p:caleb_537|Caleb⟧ son of ⟦p:jephunneh_840|Jephunneh⟧ represents Judah. ⟦p:joshua_1727|Hoshea⟧ son of ⟦p:nun_2214|Nun⟧ represents ⟦p:ephraim_1206|Ephraim⟧, and here Moses gives him the name by which he is better known, ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧, meaning the Lord saves. They are to see whether the people are strong or weak, whether the towns are walled, whether the soil is rich, and bring back some fruit. It is the season of the first ripe grapes.

For forty days they travel the length of the land, from the ⟦l:zin_1261|Wilderness of Zin⟧ in the south to ⟦l:rehob_987|Rehob⟧ in the far north. They pass through ⟦l:hebron_551|Hebron⟧, where ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧ once lived and where the patriarchs are buried, and which is now home to the descendants of ⟦p:anak_252|Anak⟧, a people remembered for their great size. The chapter ends with the spies back at ⟦l:kadesh_661|Kadesh⟧, carrying a cluster of grapes so heavy it hangs from a pole between two men, and with a report that begins well and ends in fear.
14:
The spies have given their report, and ten of them have convinced the people that ⟦l:canaan_272|Canaan⟧ cannot be taken. ⟦p:caleb_537|Caleb⟧'s attempt to quiet the crowd has failed. Now the whole congregation weeps through the night, and by morning there is talk of choosing a new leader and going back to ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧.

This is the crisis to which the whole book has been moving. ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ fall face down before the assembly. ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ and ⟦p:caleb_537|Caleb⟧ tear their clothes and plead with the people not to rebel and not to fear, because the Lord is with them. The answer is a threat to stone them.

Then the glory of the Lord appears at the Tent of Meeting. What follows echoes the golden calf at ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧, when God threatened to destroy the people and begin again with ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, and Moses interceded for them. Here Moses prays again, appealing to God's reputation among the nations and to the words God used to describe himself on the mountain: slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion. The Lord pardons, but there will be a heavy consequence, measured out in years. The chapter ends with a doomed attempt to undo the damage, on the slopes of the hill country, near a place called ⟦l:hormah_580|Hormah⟧.
15:
After the disaster at Kadesh, the book does something surprising. The narrative pauses, and the Lord gives ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ laws that begin with the words: after you enter the land that I am giving you. The generation that refused to go in has just been told they will die in the wilderness, yet the promise to their children still stands, and these instructions assume it.

The first laws concern the grain, oil and wine that are to accompany burnt offerings and sacrifices, products of a settled farming life in ⟦p:canaan_914|Canaan⟧, and the first portion of dough from each baking. Foreigners living among Israel are to bring their offerings in the same way. Then come provisions for sins committed unintentionally, by the whole community or by one person, with a sharp contrast: the one who sins defiantly, with a high hand, despises the word of the Lord.

That contrast is followed by a case from the wilderness years, a man found gathering wood on the Sabbath, which shows how seriously such defiance was treated. The chapter ends with tassels, blue cords on the corners of every garment, so that Israel will look at them and remember the commandments.
16:
The book returns to the wilderness and to the most serious challenge yet to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧. It comes from two directions at once. ⟦p:korah_1795|Korah⟧ is a Levite of the Kohathite clan, the clan entrusted with carrying the most holy things, and he is a cousin of Moses and Aaron. Alongside him stand three men from the tribe of ⟦p:reuben_2429|Reuben⟧, ⟦p:dathan_982|Dathan⟧, ⟦p:abiram_47|Abiram⟧ and On, and two hundred and fifty respected leaders of the congregation.

Their charge is that ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ have raised themselves too high, since the whole community is holy. ⟦p:korah_1795|Korah⟧'s ambition, Moses says, is the priesthood itself. ⟦p:dathan_982|Dathan⟧ and ⟦p:abiram_47|Abiram⟧ refuse even to come when summoned, and their reply turns the story upside down: it was ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧, they say, that was a land flowing with milk and honey.

⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ proposes a test. ⟦p:korah_1795|Korah⟧ and his men are to bring censers with fire and incense before the Lord, alongside ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧, and the Lord will show whom he has chosen. What follows is one of the most fearful scenes in the Torah. The next day the whole congregation turns against Moses and Aaron, and it is Aaron, censer in hand, who runs into the crowd and stands between the living and the dead.
17:
The rebellion of ⟦p:korah_1795|Korah⟧ has been crushed, but the question behind it has not gone away: who has God chosen to serve as priest? This short chapter settles it in a way no one could dispute.

Each of the twelve tribal leaders brings a staff, a walking stick or rod that served as a sign of authority, with his name written on it. ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s name is written on the staff of ⟦p:levi_1820|Levi⟧. The staffs are placed overnight in the Tent of Meeting before the ark of the Testimony, and the Lord says that the staff of the man he chooses will sprout. In the morning ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ goes in, and what he finds is more than a sprout.

⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s staff is then kept before the ark as a lasting sign for the rebellious. The chapter ends with the people overwhelmed with fear, crying out that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die. It is a real question after so many deaths, and the next chapter gives the Lord's answer.
18:
The people's frightened question at the end of the last chapter was whether anyone could come near the tabernacle and live. The Lord now answers, and this time he speaks directly to ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧.

The answer is a system of protection. ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and his sons, the priests, are to bear responsibility for the sanctuary and the altar, and to guard what lies behind the veil. Their fellow Levites will assist them and keep watch over the Tent, but they must not touch the holy furnishings or the altar. Ordinary Israelites will no longer approach. In this way the holiness of God's dwelling is guarded, so that wrath does not break out on the people again.

The second half of the chapter explains how this tribe will live, since the priests and Levites will receive no territory when the land is divided. The Lord himself is their portion. The priests receive their share of the holy offerings, the firstfruits and the redemption price of the firstborn, by what is called a covenant of salt, an image of something preserved and lasting. The Levites receive the tithes of Israel, and from those tithes they in turn give a tenth to the priests.
19:
Death has walked through the camp in the recent chapters, at ⟦l:kibroth-hattaavah_685|Kibroth-hattaavah⟧, after the spies' report and in the rebellion of ⟦p:korah_1795|Korah⟧. Under the laws of purity, anyone who touched a dead body became unclean, unable to come near the sanctuary. This chapter provides the remedy.

It begins with an unusual sacrifice. A red heifer, a young cow without defect that has never worn a yoke, is brought to ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧, ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s son, slaughtered outside the camp and burned completely, together with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet wool. Its ashes are gathered and kept outside the camp. Mixed with fresh water, they make the water of purification.

The rest of the chapter applies it. Anyone who touches a corpse, a human bone or a grave, or who is in a tent when someone dies, is unclean for seven days and must be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh days. One of the paradoxes of the ritual is that those who prepare the ashes and the water are themselves made unclean until evening. The letter to the Hebrews would later recall these ashes in its reflection on cleansing.
20:
Israel is back at ⟦l:kadesh_661|Kadesh⟧, in the ⟦l:zin_1261|Wilderness of Zin⟧. The chapter names the first month but not the year, and the long years of wandering have passed almost without a word. ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s death, at the end of this chapter, is later dated to the fortieth year after the exodus, so most of the generation that refused to enter the land is now gone. The chapter opens with another death. ⟦p:miriam_2087|Miriam⟧, the sister of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and Aaron, dies at Kadesh and is buried there.

Then comes a familiar crisis. There is no water, and the people quarrel with ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ in words that echo their parents. This time the Lord tells Moses to take the staff and speak to the rock in front of the people. What Moses does instead costs him and ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ the promised land.

The rest of the chapter turns toward the journey ahead. From ⟦l:kadesh_661|Kadesh⟧, ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ sends messengers to the king of ⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧, descended from ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧'s brother ⟦p:esau_1216|Esau⟧, asking to pass through his land along the King's Highway, the main road east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ rift. Edom refuses, and comes out with an army to make sure of it. The chapter closes on ⟦l:mount_hor_842|Mount Hor⟧, near Edom's border, where ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s priestly garments are placed on his son ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧.
21:
The new generation now begins to win battles. When the Canaanite king of ⟦l:arad_81|Arad⟧, in the ⟦l:negeb_885|Negev⟧, attacks and takes captives, Israel calls on the Lord and defeats him. The place is named ⟦l:hormah_580|Hormah⟧, the very name of the place where their parents were routed after Kadesh.

⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧'s refusal forces a long detour around its territory, and the people grow impatient and speak against God and ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, despising the manna once more. Venomous snakes appear in the camp. When the people confess, God tells Moses to make a snake and put it on a pole, so that anyone bitten may look at it and live. Centuries later, the bronze snake would be destroyed by King ⟦p:hezekiah_1512|Hezekiah⟧ because Israel had begun to worship it, and in John's Gospel ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ uses this scene to describe his own lifting up.

From here the journey moves north through the lands east of the Dead Sea, with a rapid run of place names, a fragment from an old collection called the Book of the Wars of the Lord, and a song about a well. Two kings stand in the way: ⟦p:sihon_2739|Sihon⟧, king of the ⟦p:amorite_237|Amorites⟧, whose capital is ⟦l:heshbon_565|Heshbon⟧, and ⟦p:og_2238|Og⟧, king of ⟦l:bashan_159|Bashan⟧, the fertile highland farther north. By the end of the chapter, both their lands are in Israel's hands.
22:
With ⟦p:sihon_2739|Sihon⟧ and Og defeated, Israel moves to the place where it will stay for the rest of the book and all of Deuteronomy: the plains of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, on the eastern side of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ River, opposite ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧. The camp looks across the valley at the promised land.

The Moabites, descendants of ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧'s nephew ⟦p:lot_1830|Lot⟧, watch with dread. Their king, ⟦p:balak_387|Balak⟧ son of ⟦p:zippor_3094|Zippor⟧, has seen what happened to the ⟦p:amorite_237|Amorites⟧ and does not trust his army to do better. So he turns to the spiritual weapons of his world. He sends elders of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧ and of ⟦l:midian_796|Midian⟧, Moab's neighbours, with fees for divination, to summon ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ son of ⟦p:beor_466|Beor⟧ from ⟦l:pethor_939|Pethor⟧, by the ⟦l:euphrates_421|Euphrates⟧, far away to the east. Balaam is a famous seer, and Balak believes that those he curses are cursed. A plaster inscription found at Deir Alla in ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, written some centuries later, also names a seer called Balaam son of Beor.

For the next three chapters Israel itself barely appears. The story is told from the hills of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, and it opens with ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧'s hesitation, God's warnings, and a journey interrupted by an angel with a drawn sword, which the seer cannot see but his donkey can.
23:
⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ has arrived in ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧ and been welcomed by King ⟦p:balak_387|Balak⟧, and from the heights of Bamoth-baal the two men look down on the outskirts of Israel's camp. Balak is a king paying for a curse. Balaam has already warned him that he can speak only the words God puts in his mouth.

The ritual is carefully prepared. Seven altars are built, and on each a bull and a ram are offered. ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ goes off alone to a barren height to see whether the Lord will meet him, and then he returns and speaks. His words are poetry, the first of a series of oracles, and they are not what ⟦p:balak_387|Balak⟧ paid for.

The pattern then repeats. ⟦p:balak_387|Balak⟧, unwilling to give up, takes ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ to a second vantage point, the top of ⟦l:pisgah_950|Pisgah⟧, hoping that a different view of the camp will produce a different result. Again seven altars, again the sacrifices, again a message from the Lord. The second oracle contains one of the most quoted lines of the book: God is not a man, that he should lie. By the end of the chapter, Balak is ready to try a third place, the top of ⟦l:peor_933|Peor⟧.
24:
⟦p:balak_387|Balak⟧ and ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ stand on the top of ⟦l:peor_933|Peor⟧, beside seven more altars. Something has changed in the seer. He no longer goes aside to look for omens, as he did before. He simply turns toward the wilderness, where Israel's tents are spread out tribe by tribe below him, and the ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|Spirit of God⟧ comes on him.

His third oracle is a picture of Israel flourishing, its tents spread out like gardens beside a river, and it ends with an echo of God's promise to ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧: blessed are those who bless you, and cursed are those who curse you. ⟦p:balak_387|Balak⟧ strikes his hands together in fury and dismisses him without payment.

But ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ is not finished. Before he leaves he speaks a fourth oracle, about what Israel will do to ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧ in days to come, and it looks far beyond the present moment: a star will come out of ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧, and a sceptre will rise from Israel. Its words find a first fulfilment in ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, who would one day conquer Moab and ⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧, and they point further still, to a greater king to come. Brief words follow about ⟦l:amalek_53|Amalek⟧, the Kenites and distant powers, and then the two men go their separate ways.
25:
⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧'s oracles have blessed Israel from the hills above the camp. Now the scene shifts down to the camp itself, at ⟦l:shittim_1086|Shittim⟧ on the plains of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, and what happens there is the opposite of the picture Balaam painted.

Israelite men begin to sleep with Moabite women, who invite them to the sacrifices for their gods. Soon Israel is eating the sacrifices and bowing down to ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧ of ⟦l:peor_933|Peor⟧, the Canaanite god Baal as he was worshipped at Peor. ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧'s king could not curse Israel. Israel is now bringing judgement on itself. Only later, in chapter thirty-one, does the book reveal who gave the advice behind it.

A plague breaks out in the camp. While the people weep at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, an Israelite leader openly brings a Midianite woman into his family's tent. ⟦p:phinehas_2349|Phinehas⟧, the grandson of ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ and son of the new high priest ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧, acts at once. The Lord grants Phinehas a covenant of lasting priesthood, and commands Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies. This is the last great rebellion of the wilderness years, and with it the old generation passes from the story.
26:
The plague that followed the sin at ⟦l:peor_933|Peor⟧ has ended, and the book reaches a new beginning. Almost forty years after the first census at ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧, the Lord tells ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ and ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧, now high priest in ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧'s place, to count Israel's fighting men again. The setting is the plains of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, by the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, across from ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧.

The pattern deliberately mirrors the opening of the book. Tribe by tribe, the men of twenty and over are registered, this time with the clans of each tribe named. Along the way the list pauses to remember the past: ⟦p:dathan_982|Dathan⟧ and ⟦p:abiram_47|Abiram⟧ swallowed by the earth with ⟦p:korah_1795|Korah⟧, though Korah's line did not die out; Judah's sons ⟦p:er_1209|Er⟧ and ⟦p:onan_2250|Onan⟧, who died in ⟦p:canaan_914|Canaan⟧; the five daughters of a man named ⟦p:zelophehad_3035|Zelophehad⟧, who had no sons and who will speak for themselves in the next chapter. Some tribes have grown and others shrunk, ⟦p:simeon_2741|Simeon⟧ most sharply, but the total is close to the first census.

The purpose of this count is no longer only the army. It is the inheritance, since the land is to be divided according to the size of each tribe. The chapter ends with a quiet, weighty sentence. Of all the men counted at ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧, not one remains, except ⟦p:caleb_537|Caleb⟧ son of ⟦p:jephunneh_840|Jephunneh⟧ and ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ son of ⟦p:nun_2214|Nun⟧.
27:
The new census has been taken with the division of the land in view, and that raises a practical question. Five sisters, the daughters of ⟦p:zelophehad_3035|Zelophehad⟧ of the tribe of ⟦p:manasseh_1928|Manasseh⟧, come to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting and stand before ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧, the leaders and the whole congregation. Their names are Mahlah, ⟦p:noah_2211|Noah⟧, Hoglah, Milcah and ⟦p:tirzah_2868|Tirzah⟧. Their father died in the wilderness, they explain, not as one of ⟦p:korah_1795|Korah⟧'s rebels but for his own sin, and he had no sons. Must his name disappear from his clan simply because he had daughters?

⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ takes the case to the Lord, and the answer creates a new law of inheritance for all Israel.

Then the chapter turns to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ himself. The Lord tells him to climb a mountain in the ⟦l:abarim_2|Abarim⟧ range, the heights east of the Dead Sea, and look at the land he will not enter, because of what happened at ⟦l:meribah_782|Meribah⟧. Moses' response is not a plea for himself but a prayer for the people, that they will not be like sheep without a shepherd. The Lord names his successor, ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ son of ⟦p:nun_2214|Nun⟧, a man in whom is ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧, and Moses lays his hands on him before ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧ and the whole congregation.
28:
A new leader has been commissioned, and the land is within sight. Before the conquest begins, the Lord sets out the regular offerings that Israel as a whole is to bring throughout the year. These two chapters read like a calendar of worship, a public timetable for the altar.

Many of the feasts were introduced in Exodus and Leviticus. What these chapters add is the precise list of animals, grain, oil and wine for each occasion. It begins with the daily offering, a lamb in the morning and another at twilight, the steady heartbeat of the sanctuary, first established at ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧. Then come the extra offerings for each Sabbath, for the beginning of every month at the new moon, and for the great spring festivals: Passover, on the fourteenth day of the first month, followed by the seven days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and later the Feast of Weeks, when the first of the grain harvest is brought to the Lord.

The repetition of numbers and measures is part of the point. The new generation is being told exactly how the life of worship will go on, day after day and season after season, once they are in the land.
29:
The calendar of offerings continues with the seventh month, in the autumn, the busiest month of Israel's sacred year. It opens on the first day with a sacred assembly and the sounding of trumpets. On the tenth day comes the day on which the people are to humble themselves, the Day of Atonement described in Leviticus.

Then, from the fifteenth day, comes the great harvest festival, a feast of seven days that Leviticus calls the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lived in shelters to remember the wilderness. It receives more offerings than any other occasion in the year. On its first day, thirteen bulls are offered, and the number falls by one each day, until seven are offered on the seventh day. An eighth day of solemn assembly follows.

The chapter closes by reminding Israel that these are only the fixed public offerings, in addition to everything individuals bring to fulfil their own vows or as freewill gifts.
30:
The last chapter ended with vows, and this one takes up the subject in detail. ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ speaks to the heads of the tribes about promises made to the Lord.

The principle is stated first, simply and absolutely. When a man makes a vow or binds himself by an oath, he must not break his word. Then the chapter works through the situation of a woman, whose vow could affect the household she belonged to in that society. A young woman still living in her father's house, a wife, and a widow or divorced woman are each considered in turn. A father or husband who hears of a vow may cancel it on the day he hears it, and if he does, the Lord releases her. If he says nothing, it stands. A widow or divorced woman answers for her own vows.

The chapter is brief and legal in tone. Set between the commissioning of ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ and the war against Midian, it reflects how seriously Israel was to treat words spoken before God.
31:
Back in chapter twenty-five, after the sin at ⟦l:peor_933|Peor⟧, the Lord told ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ to treat the Midianites as enemies. Now the order comes to carry it out, and with it a sobering note: after this, Moses will be gathered to his people. It is the last campaign he will oversee.

A thousand men are sent from each tribe, twelve thousand in all. They are accompanied not by ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ but by ⟦p:phinehas_2349|Phinehas⟧ the priest, carrying holy articles and the trumpets for signalling, a sign that this is the Lord's battle. Among the dead are five kings of ⟦l:midian_796|Midian⟧ and, unexpectedly, ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ son of ⟦p:beor_466|Beor⟧. Only now does the book reveal that it was Balaam's counsel that led Israel astray at ⟦l:peor_933|Peor⟧. The seer who could not curse Israel found another way to harm them.

When the army returns with its captives, ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ goes out to meet it, and his orders are severe. The rest of the chapter deals with the aftermath: purifying the soldiers and their spoils, dividing the plunder between the fighters and the whole community, with a share for the priests and Levites, and an offering of gold from commanders who find that not one of their men is missing.
32:
Israel now holds the lands east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ taken from ⟦p:sihon_2739|Sihon⟧ and ⟦p:og_2238|Og⟧, and two tribes look at them with a herdsman's eye. The tribes of ⟦p:reuben_2429|Reuben⟧ and ⟦p:gad_1262|Gad⟧ have very large herds and flocks, and the territory of ⟦l:jazer_628|Jazer⟧ and ⟦l:gilead_475|Gilead⟧, the high pastureland east of the river, is ideal for livestock. They come to ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧ and the leaders with a request: let us settle here, and do not make us cross the Jordan.

To ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ it sounds dangerously familiar. He hears in it an echo of ⟦l:kadesh-barnea_663|Kadesh-barnea⟧, when the spies discouraged the people and a whole generation was lost, and his reply is stern. Are your brothers to go to war while you sit here?

In the negotiation that follows, the two tribes offer a solemn promise, and ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ sets the terms, warning them that their sin will find them out if they fail. The arrangement is passed on to ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧ and to ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧, who will see it carried out. By the end of the chapter, half of the tribe of ⟦p:manasseh_1928|Manasseh⟧ has been included too, and these eastern lands will become the homeland of two and a half tribes of Israel.
33:
As the long march nears its end, the book pauses to look back over the whole route. At the Lord's command, the chapter says, ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ recorded the stages of Israel's journey, and here they are, from ⟦l:rameses_980|Rameses⟧ in ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ to the plains of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧.

It begins with the night of the exodus, when Israel marched out boldly while the Egyptians buried their firstborn. Then it lists the camps one by one: ⟦l:succoth_1114|Succoth⟧, the crossing of the sea, ⟦l:marah_765|Marah⟧ and ⟦l:elim_369|Elim⟧, ⟦l:sinai_1098|Sinai⟧, and on through some forty stopping places. Many of these names appear nowhere else in Scripture. They fill in the long years that the story itself passed over in silence. The list pauses only once, for the death of ⟦p:aaron_1|Aaron⟧ on ⟦l:mount_hor_842|Mount Hor⟧, in the fortieth year after the exodus, at the age of a hundred and twenty-three.

When the itinerary reaches the plains of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, the chapter turns from the past to the future. The Lord gives instructions for the land across the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧: drive out its inhabitants, destroy their idols and high places, and divide the land by lot. And there is a warning. Any who are allowed to remain will become barbs in Israel's eyes and thorns in their sides.
34:
The Lord has told Israel to take possession of the land and divide it by lot. Now he draws its borders, as if tracing a map for a people who have never lived there.

The southern border runs from the ⟦l:zin_1261|Wilderness of Zin⟧ along the edge of ⟦l:edom_357|Edom⟧, from the southern end of the ⟦l:salt_sea_1021|Salt Sea⟧, which we call the ⟦l:salt_sea_1021|Dead Sea⟧, past ⟦l:kadesh-barnea_663|Kadesh-barnea⟧ and along the ⟦l:egypt_259|Brook of Egypt⟧, a seasonal stream bed in the desert, to the Mediterranean, here called the ⟦l:great_sea_493|Great Sea⟧. The coast forms the western border. The northern line runs from the sea toward ⟦l:lebo-hamath_723|Lebo-hamath⟧, in the region of modern ⟦l:lebanon_720|Lebanon⟧ and ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧, and the eastern border comes down past the Sea of Chinnereth, later known as the ⟦l:sea_of_galilee_1032|Sea of Galilee⟧, and along the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ back to the Salt Sea. The outline is clear. This is the land west of the Jordan, for the nine and a half tribes still waiting for their share.

The chapter ends with the men who will oversee the division: ⟦p:eleazar_1062|Eleazar⟧ the priest and ⟦p:joshua_1727|Joshua⟧ son of ⟦p:nun_2214|Nun⟧, with a leader from each tribe. Among the tribal leaders only one name is familiar. Representing Judah, as he did among the spies almost forty years before, is ⟦p:caleb_537|Caleb⟧ son of ⟦p:jephunneh_840|Jephunneh⟧.
35:
The land has been mapped, and each tribe will receive its share. But the Levites, as the book has already explained, will receive no territory of their own. Instead, this chapter provides them with towns to live in, forty-eight in all, scattered through the lands of the other tribes, each with pastureland around it for their herds and flocks.

Six of these Levite towns are to serve a special purpose. They will be cities of refuge, three east of the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ and three in ⟦p:canaan_914|Canaan⟧. In the ancient world, when someone was killed, it fell to a close relative, called the avenger of blood, to take the life of the killer. These cities offer protection to a person who has killed someone by accident, until the community can hear the case.

The chapter draws careful distinctions between murder and accidental killing: the weapon used, whether there was hostility, whether it was planned. The one who killed unintentionally must stay in the city of refuge until the death of the high priest. Behind it all lies a conviction stated in the final lines, that bloodshed pollutes the land, and this is the land where the Lord himself will dwell among his people.
36:
The book ends by returning to the five daughters of ⟦p:zelophehad_3035|Zelophehad⟧, whose request for their father's land was granted in chapter twenty-seven. Now the leaders of their clan, the family of ⟦p:gilead_1317|Gilead⟧ in the tribe of ⟦p:manasseh_1928|Manasseh⟧, raise a further question.

If these women marry men from other tribes, the land they inherit will pass with their children to those tribes, and ⟦p:manasseh_1928|Manasseh⟧'s territory will shrink. Even the Jubilee, the fiftieth year when land returned to its original family, would not bring it back, because it would by then belong to another tribe by inheritance. The concern is for each tribe to keep the land God gives it.

⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ brings the answer from the Lord. The daughters may marry whoever they please, as long as they marry within their father's tribe. They do, marrying cousins on their father's side. It is a quiet ending to a book of turbulent events, and it looks forward with confidence. The land has not yet been entered, yet its future ownership is already being settled. The last sentence places these laws where the whole second half of the book has stood: on the plains of ⟦l:moab_815|Moab⟧, by the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, across from ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧.
